To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The ODIT (occupational disease information tool) consists of nine indicators and criteria to assess the ability of registries to provide appropriate information on the incidence and prevalence of occupational diseases for preventive policy on the national level.
the indicators completeness of notification form, completeness of registration and presentation of monitor information have a good content validity.

we have developed nine quality indicators for the evaluation of the ability of a registry to provide appropriate information to support preventive policy on a nation level, and that all indicators met the preset criteria of content validity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what constitutes a good quality registry for occupational disease.
the quality of registries of work-related diseases, and the indicators and criteria developed can be used for the assessment of the quality of these registries.
the question how to assess the quality of a registry for occupational diseases in relation with its use for preventive policy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ODIT is a tool for assessing the quality of registries for occupational disease in terms of the quality of their information output for the purpose of preventive policy.
the ODIT can be used to evaluate the quality of national occupational disease registries with respect to their capacity to provide appropriate information in the field of prevention.
the indicators are useful to determine the quality of registries for occupational disease in relation to preventive policies on a national level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the quality of registries can best be evaluated by looking at the completeness of the registration form, the guidelines for notification, the completeness of the registry, the statistical methods used, the investigation of special cases and the presentation of the information.
the development of a quality tool to evaluate registries of occupational disease is a useful exercise, but that it is not easy.

the quality of the registry is determined by the completeness of notification, completeness of registration and the statistical methods used, and by the guidelines or criteria for the notification, education and the training of the reporting physicians, investigation of special notification cases and presentation of the results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
registries should provide monitor and alert information, and that the completeness of the registration forms is of utmost importance.
the development of quality indicators and criteria is a process in which all stakeholders should be involved.
registries for occupational disease are not only a tool to monitor and alert, but also a tool to improve prevention.
